title: Taizé chant
hookLine: a short line sung over and over until it sings you

cards: How many times can a person sing the same line before it stops being words? In a small village in France there's a monastic community called Taizé, brothers from different churches living under one rule.
Young people travel there to stay for a week, and in the evening they crowd into a long, low-lit church and sit on the floor. There's no sermon to speak of.
A few voices start a line, short enough to learn in one hearing, and everyone joins. Then again. And again.
Somewhere along the way, some who sing it say, you stop singing the line and it starts singing you.

teach.b: A Taizé chant is built small on purpose. One line, from scripture or an old prayer, set to a simple tune and sung over and over, sometimes with harmony underneath and a single voice rising above.
The words come in Latin, in English, in other languages, so people who don't share a language can share a line. One chant sets the words of the thief crucified beside Jesus.
In Luke's Gospel he says: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." That's the whole prayer. Sung slowly, many times, it has room to sink in.
Didn't Jesus say, in the King James words, "use not vain repetitions"? He did. The same verse says what he's warning against: those who "think that they shall be heard for their much speaking."
Many readers, including those who sing at Taizé, take the problem to be the vain, not the repeated, and point to Matthew's own Gospel.
In Gethsemane, on his last night, Jesus prays to let the cup pass, comes back, prays again, and then "prayed the third time, saying the same words." On his hardest night, he repeated himself.
Here's why it can rest a person. When the line doesn't change, the mind can stop straining for the next word, or performing, or keeping up.

The line carries you, the way a boat carries someone who has finally stopped rowing. And it can surface later, at a red light or over a sink full of dishes: a prayer that keeps going after the singing stops.

how: At Taizé, and in churches and student groups that borrow its style, prayer services center on short chants sung many times over, with scripture readings and a long silence, often by candlelight.

s: a Taizé chant is a long hymn with many verses
it's one short line, sung over and over.
in Gethsemane, Jesus prays the same words more than once
he "prayed the third time, saying the same words."
Jesus's warning in Matthew 6 is against praying any words twice
the warning is against vain repetitions, heaping up words to be heard.

games.q: it's Jesus's last night, in Gethsemane. he has prayed, found his friends asleep, and prayed again. he goes back a third time. what does he pray?
o: a new prayer, with new words.
games.why: Matthew says he "prayed the third time, saying the same words." on his hardest night, he repeated himself.

practice: Choose a short line: if you pray, it could be the thief's, Lord, remember me; if not, any line that matters to you.

Sing it quietly ten times on any simple tune, or just hum it, letting your fingers keep count, and if your mind wanders, simply come back to the line. After the tenth, stop, and let the quiet hold what's left.

wordCard.voice: Taizé chant. A short line of scripture or prayer, sung over and over, from a monastic community in France.

orig.note: Greek: to babble, to heap up empty words. Matthew 6:7, rendered use not vain repetitions.

carryVoice: Your line: repetition is rest. Not vain words, just the same words, said again. Until tomorrow.
